plants.name: Solidago canadensis
plants.description: Dense, feathery plumes of tiny golden flowers rise above meadows, roadsides and prairie edges. They glow in late-summer light and hum with bees, butterflies and hoverflies stocking up for autumn.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to autumn, typically July through October, with a peak in late August and September
plants.location: Eastern and central North America, including the Great Lakes region and northeastern United States and southeastern Canada
plants.funFact: Goldenrod is often blamed for hay fever, but its pollen is heavy and sticky and spreads by insects. The real culprit is usually ragweed, which blooms at the same time and releases pollen into the air.

plants.name: Calluna vulgaris
plants.description: Moorlands and heaths across northern Europe turn into rolling carpets of purple. Each wiry stem is covered in tiny bell-shaped blossoms, and the hills look as if they have been brushed with violet.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer into autumn, roughly August through September and sometimes into October
plants.location: Moorlands and heathlands of the British Isles, Scandinavia and northern and western Europe, including the Scottish Highlands
plants.funFact: Heather honey is prized for its thick, jelly-like texture. Beekeepers sometimes move their hives onto the moors at this time of year so the bees can feed on the bloom.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Australia's national floral emblem bursts into fluffy, golden pom-pom blossoms at the end of winter. Its branches fill with sweetly scented flower balls that brighten the bush, and the display is celebrated on Wattle Day.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to spring in the Southern Hemisphere, around July through October and peaking in August and September
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including Victoria, South Australia and New South Wales
plants.funFact: Australia celebrates National Wattle Day on September 1, the first day of spring. The golden and green of the Australian sporting colors come from the wattle's blossoms and leaves.
